rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the eight-compound elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to tune selectivity in either direction.

Only the first pair limits the score, while the last peak already elutes before 10 minutes. Raising temperature with the gradient unchanged tests whether temperature-dependent selectivity can resolve that pair without a time penalty.
Lengthen only the gradient to test whether the limiting first pair responds to slope. The current 6.90-minute last peak leaves room to gain resolution while targeting elution within 10 minutes.

The shallower gradient brought the first pair close to full resolution, and higher temperature previously improved its separation. Raising temperature to 60 C may lift that pair above R = 1.5 while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.

The maximum CRF is achieved, so shorten the gradient by one grid step to seek a faster fully resolved method. Keep the solvent window and temperature fixed to isolate the effect on the two closest pairs.

Shorten the gradient another two minutes while retaining the favorable temperature. The limiting first pair still has resolution margin at R = 1.91, so this tests a faster method without sacrificing full separation.
Test the next shorter gradient to locate the speed limit for the first pair, now at R = 1.67. If its resolution falls below 1.5, the 12-minute gradient remains a fully resolved fallback.

Lowering phi1 makes the slope equivalent to an 11.25-minute full-window gradient, between the resolved and slightly unresolved runs. The last peak previously eluted near phi = 0.58, so this endpoint should preserve gradient elution while targeting full resolution faster than injection 6.

Shift the solvent window upward while preserving injection 8's slope to test whether the initial low-organic segment can be trimmed. This should shorten retention, but the first pair must be checked because its resolution margin is small.

Test the low-temperature endpoint for a different selectivity regime: because peaks have no identities, the first pair may have reversed order between 40 and 55 C. Lower temperature could therefore separate it more strongly, while the broad gradient should keep the final peak near the 10-minute target.

Use a slope between injections 7 and 8 to target first-pair resolution just above 1.5 with a shorter gradient. The final peak may elute shortly into the 0.55 hold, so this run will check whether the lower endpoint preserves the time advantage.

Test whether a steeper gradient separates the late cluster seen at 25 C while retaining adequate resolution of the first pair. This explores a potentially faster low-temperature alternative, with injection 11 retained as the fastest fully resolved method so far.

The late cluster barely responded to gradient slope at 25 C, so test a modest temperature increase to change its selectivity. An eight-minute gradient balances the strong low-temperature separation of the first pair against faster elution.

Return to the fastest fully resolved regime and raise phi0 by one step while keeping the endpoint and gradient duration fixed. The resulting shallower slope may offset the first-pair resolution loss from the higher starting organic fraction and shorten elution further.

Reduce the slope to 0.07 organic fraction per minute to recover the small first-pair resolution deficit at phi0 = 0.10. The higher endpoint keeps the last peak inside the gradient, testing a fully resolved alternative near seven minutes.

Test an intermediate temperature to separate the late cluster, with a higher starting organic fraction to shorten the low-temperature run. This also checks whether shifting the solvent window improves the early pair's selectivity in this temperature regime.

Test a slightly shallower slope than injection 11 with an endpoint high enough to keep the last peak inside the gradient. This targets maximum CRF near seven minutes with a little more first-pair resolution margin and no final-peak hold elution.

Make the gradient shallower than injection 16 to test whether its limiting first pair can reach full resolution at 35 C. The late pairs already have adequate separation, and the last peak should remain below 10 minutes.

Test a slope just steeper than the fastest fully resolved method to locate the first-pair resolution boundary more precisely. The higher endpoint avoids hold elution and may shorten the last-peak time, though the first pair is likely to be borderline.

Test a higher starting organic fraction with a substantially shallower slope to see whether early-pair resolution can be recovered while trimming initial retention. Injection 11 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Fine-tune the slope just above injection 15's fully resolved setting to test a small retention-time reduction at phi0 = 0.10. This should put the first pair close to R = 1.5 while keeping all peaks inside the gradient.

With maximum CRF already secured, test a more balanced resolution margin between the first and third pairs using a slope slightly shallower than injection 5. This should retain elution below 10 minutes while providing a less borderline alternative to the fastest method.

Preserve injection 6's fully resolving slope while trimming the unused high-organic end of its programmed gradient. The last peak is expected near 7.49 minutes, before the gradient ends at the outlet, retaining maximum CRF with more resolution margin than injection 11.

Trim injection 15's solvent window and gradient duration while making its slope slightly shallower to protect the limiting first pair. This targets maximum CRF with all peaks eluting during the gradient and a shorter programmed gradient than injection 15.

Use the final injection to test a compact solvent window with a slope expected to preserve full resolution and keep the last peak below 10 minutes. Injection 11 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method; this alternative targets greater resolution margin.
